title: Named retro games discovery
summary: Review five projects for Bloodwych, Nebulus, Neuromancer and Head over Heels.
notes: Personally reviewed pinned upstream READMEs and checked current catalogue search; no independent builds or binary comparisons.

bloodwych-atari-st-bw-dataviewer-readme.text:
# Bloodwych Data Viewer

## Why

I did an IFF parser for audio/video a while back. See https://drsnuggles.github.io/IFF/

But there was no viewer for Bloodwych GFX files which are Atari ST raw file format.

Thanks to https://github.com/HoraceAndTheSpider/Bloodwych-68k/wiki i could manage to change that.

## GFX

Thats the new part done here.

## SFX

For playing back sounds i use my IFF/8SVX lib back from 2020.

## License
Public Domain

head-over-heels-cpc-hohpc-readme.text:
﻿# Head over Heels — reconstrucción nativa para PC

Estado: **prototipo técnico, no réplica completa del juego**.

La aplicación Windows dibuja datos extraídos de `Head over Heels (Europe).dsk`
y traduce reglas de movimiento, salto, unión, bolsa y disparo a C#. No contiene un
intérprete Z80, emulador de CPC, ROM ni dependencia de un emulador instalado.

## Ejecutar

Abrir `build/actual/HeadOverHeelsPC.exe` o `Jugar.cmd`. Requiere Windows y .NET Desktop
Runtime 10, disponible en el equipo utilizado para compilar.

- WASD o flechas: movimiento paralelo a las paredes. Arriba/W: arriba-derecha;
  abajo/S: abajo-izquierda; izquierda/A: arriba-izquierda; derecha/D: abajo-derecha.
- Espacio: salto.
- Espacio sobre una plataforma de teletransporte: activar su ruta original.
- Tab: cambiar de personaje.
- Tab cuando Head está sobre Heels: unirlos; Tab de nuevo: separarlos.
- E: recoger/dejar un objeto con la bolsa de Heels.
- F o Ctrl: disparar con Head, si tiene bocina y munición.
- R: nueva partida.
- M: activar/silenciar los efectos de sonido sintetizados.
- F2: vista de nueve posiciones de habitación en la misma planta.
- RePág / AvPág: recorrer las habitaciones recuperadas en el visor.
- Esc: pausa. F11: pantalla completa.

El mapa es un visor de datos: una posición vacía indica que no hay una habitación
recuperada en esas coordenadas. Hay reglas de movimiento discreto, colisiones,
inventario, daño y varias familias de enemigos portadas desde el Z80; todavía
necesitan contrastarse durante partidas completas.

## Recuperación reproducible

`python tools/recover.py` lee el DSK original y genera `assets/world.json`,
`assets/provenance.json` y `analysis/relocated.bin`. Usa solamente Python 3 y
su biblioteca estándar. No ejecuta código del juego.

Se recuperan cuatro archivos AMSDOS, 301 registros de habitaciones con objetos
y macros expandidas, 100 entradas gráficas, 52 registros de coleccionables,
paredes y ocho paletas originales. Los identificadores
y direcciones originales se conservan para contrastar cada hallazgo.

## Compilar y comprobar

Ejecutar `Compilar.cmd`. Requiere Python 3 y el SDK de .NET 10.

`build/actual/HeadOverHeelsPC.exe --verify` dibuja todas las habitaciones, comprueba
salto/aterrizaje nativos y separación de personajes, y guarda imágenes e informe
en `build/actual/verification`. Son comprobaciones de funcionamiento del prototipo;
**no demuestran equivalencia con el original**.

## Estructura

- `src/World.cs`: datos inmutables y estado independiente por habitación.
- `src/NativeGame.cs`: personajes, colisiones, inventario, daño y proyectiles.
- `src/ObjectBehaviors.cs`: familias de movimiento recuperadas.
- `src/OriginalRandom.cs`: generador aleatorio original traducido a C#.
- `src/Renderer.cs`: dibujo por habitación, independiente de la simulación.
- `src/Program.cs`: ventana, entrada de teclado y composición de varias cámaras.
- `tools/recover.py`: lectura del disco y conversión estática de datos.
- `analysis/INVESTIGACION.md`: evidencia, límites y trabajo pendiente.

## Pendiente para replicar el juego

Faltan variantes de cambios verticales y caídas, interacciones completas entre cuerpos,
interruptores y varias familias de objetos, música y menús originales.
El suelo usa los patrones recuperados del disco; la selección de variantes de pared y
partes de puerta está incompleta. La colisión compuesta, los checkpoints y la
respuesta exacta a todas las interacciones necesitan más reconstrucción.

Se portaron el ciclo nominal de 80 ms, pasos distintos de Head/Heels, ascenso
discreto, unión, bolsa, requisitos de bocina/munición y congelación de enemigos
elegibles. Los coleccionables y coronas se leen de su tabla independiente. Las
familias móviles implementadas cubren rebotes, giros, cambios aleatorios y
persecución; no representan todavía todos los 37 comportamientos originales.

Las 482 puertas visibles recuperadas tienen destino y retorno comprobados.
Se recuperaron 22 parejas de teletransporte; se conserva el orden original
de búsqueda y los contadores de 12 ticks de salida y 8 de llegada. Estas pruebas
comprueban los datos y reglas portados, sin certificar todavía una partida completa.

`analysis/CHARACTERS-Z80.md`, `OBJECTS-Z80.md`, `SPRITE-COLOR-Z80.md`,
`BEHAVIORS-Z80.md` y `PROJECTILES-Z80.md` registran direcciones y límites.
La referencia emulada en `analysis/reference` se utiliza solo durante desarrollo.

Las habitaciones tienen estado propio y el renderizador recibe una habitación
explícita. Por ello la futura vista de varias salas no depende de alterar una
pantalla o memoria global de CPC.

Los gráficos y datos se obtienen del disco facilitado por el usuario. Créditos
del original: Jon Ritman, Bernie Drummond, Guy Stevens y Ocean Software.

## Audio y perspectiva

Se ha sustituido el audio provisional por un secuenciador nativo y tablas de
efectos extraídas del disco CPC. Hay once asignaciones verificadas: pasos, salto,
aterrizaje, daño, teletransporte, muelle, plataforma, disparo, recogida,
equipamiento y bolsa. M permite silenciarlos. El cambio de personaje queda mudo mientras no se identifique su correspondencia
original. Los pasos se detienen al parar, saltar o pausar.
La síntesis AY y las prioridades completas todavía requieren comparación con el
original; no se presenta el audio como idéntico. Ver `analysis/original-audio.md`.

El orden de dibujo usa los volúmenes de objetos y personajes. Las escenas de
escalones y teletransportador se guardan con `--verify`; los ascensores disponen
de margen superior para que el personaje no desaparezca al subir.

`Jugar.cmd` abre `build/actual/HeadOverHeelsPC.exe`; `Compilar.cmd` genera esa
misma ruta. La carpeta permite mantener abierta la compilación anterior mientras
se prepara esta revisión. Para usar los cambios, cierra la partida anterior
cuando quieras y vuelve a abrir `Jugar.cmd`.

## Vista de juego y cámara

La cabecera compacta deja más espacio para jugar y conserva la columna del otro
personaje. Las habitaciones visitadas permanecen en un espacio isométrico común;
al cruzar una puerta la cámara se desplaza suavemente hacia la nueva habitación.
El teletransporte y el cambio de personaje también desplazan la cámara según las
coordenadas del destino. Las plantas tienen separación vertical y las coordenadas
originales de 16 sectores se desenvuelven al descubrir salas. F2 conserva el visor.
La separación entre sectores es fija: las salas pequeñas mantienen espacio entre
ellas. `--verify` comprueba orientación, estabilidad al regresar y llegada de la
cámara tras un teletransporte, y genera `camera-transition.png`.

## Empujar objetos

Camina contra un objeto móvil para empujarlo, sin tecla adicional ni bolsa.
Head, Heels y ambos unidos pueden desplazar el muelle y los otros cuerpos pasivos
identificados por sus comportamientos originales: 11 tipos, 172 objetos del mapa.
Las paredes, los obstáculos y el otro personaje bloquean el empuje. Las posiciones
se conservan en la habitación. Recoger con E sigue requiriendo la bolsa y un objeto
transportable. La inercia del original sigue siendo parcial. Evidencia y alcance
en `analysis/PUSHING-Z80.md`.

## Muelles, ascensores y salas superpuestas

Al pulsar salto sobre un muelle, Heels obtiene 8 ticks de ascenso y Head o la
pareja unida 10; también se conserva la mejora de salto de Heels y el límite de
10 ticks del original. El muelle muestra compresión y recuperación.

Las plataformas verticales de conductas 16/18/23 suben y bajan y llevan al
personaje apoyado. La plataforma de 6160 permite subir a la sala 6150: espera
hasta arriba y salta con el perro. El hueco de 6150 también permite caer a 6160.
La cámara sitúa la planta superior por encima de la inferior.

`analysis/RECUPERAR-MECANICAS.md` explica cómo se extraen y contrastan las reglas;
`analysis/BEHAVIOR-AUDIT.md` inventaría las 37 familias y sus lagunas. La revisión
corrige persecución diagonal de la familia 33, selección de eje de la 15 y orden
de consulta aleatoria. Siguen pendientes interruptores, cintas, desapariciones y
otras interacciones: dibujar todas las habitaciones no acredita el juego completo.

Los coleccionables aplican gravedad desde su posición inicial y descansan sobre
los objetos de la sala. La bocina de 3060 cae hasta la columna de altura 3 y se
recoge por contacto físico. Bolsa y bocina se adquieren para el inventario común;
su uso sigue correspondiendo respectivamente a Heels y Head. Para disparar con
Head hacen falta también munición y F/Ctrl. `--verify` comprueba la recogida en
esa sala y el disparo posterior y genera `hooter-before.png`/`hooter-collected.png`.

La salida mantiene tres bloques PCM en cola y actualiza el secuenciador a 50 Hz.
`build/actual/HeadOverHeelsPC.exe --verify-audio-timing` mide durante tres segundos
la posición real del dispositivo, sin emitir sonido, y guarda `audio-timing.json`.
Comprueba que la velocidad queda dentro del 5 % de las 22.050 muestras/segundo.


## Detalles visuales y sonido (23/10/2026)

Los ocho patrones de suelo se recuperan directamente del disco. El tipo 6
muestra pinchos y mata al tocar el suelo; los objetos y plataformas que sirven
de apoyo permiten pasar por encima. El tipo 7 conserva el hueco de ca?da.
La muerte reproduce su secuencia original de doce actualizaciones y despu?s
resta la vida; el retorno usa la entrada de cada personaje o el checkpoint.
Los coleccionables mantienen su animaci?n ocho actualizaciones al recogerse.
El transporte con bolsa conserva la retirada inmediata del original.

El muelle conserva sus sprites originales de compresi?n y recuperaci?n
43/44/43/44/43. Las puertas elevadas muestran sus apoyos originales y las
aperturas posteriores dejan de mostrar ladrillos en el interior. El recorte
del hueco es una adaptaci?n geom?trica nativa; las variantes completas de
pared siguen pendientes. Se corrigi? adem?s la rotaci?n del control de ruido AY,
que dejaba un tono a?adido en algunos efectos.

`--verify` genera l?minas de suelos, puertas, muerte, muelle y recogida en
`build/actual/verification`. La evidencia se recoge en
`analysis/VISUALS-Z80.md`. Las pruebas cubren l?gica, datos y salida gr?fica;
no certifican fidelidad audiovisual completa frente al v?deo.


El teletransporte reproduce la desaparici?n de12 ticks y la aparici?n de8
con sus tablas originales, tambi?n con los dos personajes unidos. La salida
y llegada usan los grupos sonoros C7/C8; el sonido47 permanece como ambiente
de la plataforma. La verificaci?n genera `teleport-animation.png` y comprueba
los16 efectos de sonido recuperados mediante `tools/verify_audio.py`.


## Salas largas y pasos continuos

Las salidas de c?digo1 unen registros en una misma sala visible. La4260 y
la4360 se muestran juntas, con sus dos filas de seis objetos, sin pared
intermedia. La c?mara mantiene el mismo centro al pasar de una mitad a otra.
El movimiento y el salto pueden cruzar toda la uni?n, sin exigir la apertura
estrecha de una puerta. El visor y la miniatura tambi?n encuadran el conjunto.
`--verify` comprueba los enlaces continuos y genera `room-4260-complete.png`
y `room-4260-window.png`. El estado de cada registro sigue siendo independiente.

neuromancer-iigs-mac68k-readme.text: # Neuromancer for 68K Macintosh **Chiba City, on a classic Mac.** A native 68K Macintosh adaptation of *Neuromancer*, based on the Apple IIGS game. Explore the city, follow conversations and clues, connect to databases, and confront ICE and AI in cyberspace—with a Macintosh interface designed for a 512 × 342 screen. **v0.0.2 · Monochrome & Color** [Downloads / Releases](https://github.com/apple2forever/neuromancer-mac68k/releases) · [한국어](README.ko.md) · [Report an issue](https://github.com/apple2forever/neuromancer-mac68k/issues) | Color | Monochrome | | :---: | :---: | | ![Color title screen](screenshots/color-title.png) | ![Monochrome title screen](screenshots/mono-title.png) | | Apple IIGS color artwork | Dedicated 1-bit artwork | ## Two editions, one journey - **Color:** original Apple IIGS scene artwork, displayed with Color QuickDraw. - **Monochrome:** separately redrawn black-and-white scenes using solid shapes, dots and hatching. The artwork is not a runtime-dithered version of the color images. - **Macintosh controls:** clickable icons with a pressed state, directional exit cursors, speech bubbles, and standard file menus and dialogs. - **Cyberspace:** perspective 3D navigation, an optional 2D map, and dedicated ICE / AI combat controls. - **Progress:** New Game, Open, Save and Save As, with confirmation before discarding unsaved progress. The implemented campaign runs from Chatsubo to the final encounter and ending. The adaptation is still being refined; reports of bugs and differences from the original are welcome. ## Screenshots Actual emulator captures. Screenshots show the game content at its native pixel dimensions; desktop borders have been cropped. Click an image to view it separately. | | Color | Monochrome | | :--- | :---: | :---: | | **Conversations** | ![Color conversation at the Body Shop](screenshots/color-dialogue.png) | ![Monochrome conversation at the Body Shop](screenshots/mono-dialogue.png) | | **Cyberspace** | ![Color perspective cyberspace navigation](screenshots/color-cyberspace.png) | ![Monochrome perspective cyberspace navigation](screenshots/mono-cyberspace.png) | | **AI combat** | ![Color AI combat interface](screenshots/color-combat.png) | ![Monochrome AI combat interface](screenshots/mono-combat.png) | ## Download and play Get the disk images from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/apple2forever/neuromancer-mac68k/releases). | Edition | Release asset | | :--- | :--- | | Color | `Neuromancer-v0.0.2-Color.dsk` | | Monochrome | `Neuromancer-v0.0.2-Monochrome.dsk` | 1. Boot your Macintosh or emulator into a compatible System 6 or System 7 installation. 2. Mount the appropriate DSK image. Each is a **1.44 MB HFS installation image**, containing the game application only. 3. Copy the application to your Mac hard disk using the Finder, then launch **Neuromancer**. 4. Choose **New Game**, or **Open Game…** to continue an existing save. Save to a writable Mac volume. The images are **not boot disks**. Mac system software, ROMs and save files are not included. Copying inside the classic Mac Finder preserves the application's resource fork. Image-mounting support depends on your emulator. ## Tested configurations | Edition | Macintosh / RAM | System | Emulator | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Monochrome | Macintosh Plus / 4 MB | 6.0.8 | PCE | | Color | Macintosh IIx / 8 MB | 6.0.8 | MAME | | Color | Macintosh LC III / 8 MB | 7.1.1 | MAME | These are tested configurations, not a guarantee for every Mac or emulator. The color edition needs **Color QuickDraw**. The interface is designed for **512 × 342**; the game content inside its window is 500 × 295. For System 7 / MultiFinder, keep the app's memory settings at **1,536 KB minimum / 2,048 KB preferred**. These are application memory settings, not the total RAM required by the Mac. ## Controls | Action | Control | | :--- | :--- | | Move around the city | Hover over a reachable scene edge for an arrow cursor, then click. `W A S D` / arrow keys also work. | | Talk / continue | Click **Talk** or press `T`. Click an open speech bubble or press `Return` to continue. Some NPCs speak automatically on arrival. | | Choose a reply | `Space` cycles thoughts; `Return` says the selected reply. Number keys select a reply directly. Choice changes and confirmation have short sound cues. | | Move in 3D cyberspace | `W A S D`: forward / left / back / right, relative to your facing. `Q / E`: turn. `V`: switch to the 2D map. | | Fight ICE / AI | Click an action or press `1–6` to execute it. `I`: software. `S`: skills. `L`: combat log. | | Save / open / quit | `Command-S` / `Command-O` / `Command-Q`. `Shift-Command-S`: Save As. | | Full help | **Help → Controls…**, or `Command-H`. | ## Credits Original game: **Interplay, 1988**, based on the novel by **William Gibson**. The Macintosh adaptation is built with **Retro68**. This is an unofficial fan project, not an official release by the original creators. This repository contains the project introduction and screenshots; playable builds are distributed through Releases.

neuromancer-dos-javamancer-readme.text:
# javamancer A restoration of ***Neuromancer*** *PC Game (1989)* with a *Game Assets Browser*, written entirely in *Java/JavaFX*.

Click Here for More Screenshots!!! ## State of the Development ### Next Steps - **Development Pause** - Taking a break from dev. until about May 2026 - Revamp save game directory location. - Support Windows and Linux game save. - Begin testing on Windows and Linux. - Check off all cyberspace databases tested to 100% - Fix some documented GIT issue bugs. ### 2026 . February . Alpha 2 - Game Winnable! Final scenes added. - Still "late-alpha" quality but Essentially playable! - Testers invited to play and comment. - Many small game features still to test and implement. ### 2026 . January . Alpha 1 - Game Running. "late-alpha" quiality. Largely playable! - Curious testers invited to play and comment. - No downloadable version. Use NetBeans IDE please. - MacOS only. Adventurous coders wanted to adapt it to Linux or Windows. Inspired by the [Reuromancer Windows64](https://github.com/HenadziMatuts/Reuromancer) port by [Henadzi Matuts]( https://github.com/HenadziMatuts) with asset decoding/unpacking code adapted to Java/JavaFX. ## Requirements - This engine will require the original *NEURO1.DAT* and *NEURO2.DAT* resource files from the original floppies to operate. You can obtain a copy via by searching the internet. - The Java code is a cleanroom replacement for the NEURO.EXE game engine from the oroiginal disks. - For now, under development and requires NetBeans IDE for running (unless you have Maven skills). - The "Game Mode" is now playable at a late-Alpha quality. You should be able to create a character and acheive many of the game goals. Game save mostly works. Cyberspace exploration and battles are somewhat working. - Docoder wheel screen is present but can be bypassed by simply pressing ENTER. - For now the game is ***MacOS only*** (because of game save and caching files location). I'm planning on Windows and Linux integration (or if you want to contribute). ## What is *Neuromancer PC*? *Neuromancer PC* was a “1989 Game of the Year" for PCs and shipped in a [22cm x 22cm x 2cm thick box](neuro-game-box.md). The box contained a simple manual, two game floppies and a "decoder" wheel. The decoder wheel was used as DRM(copy protection). As the floppies could be easily copied, the designers of the game created an interactive wheel to use during the "on-line" portion of the game. The user would be presented with a three word phrase and would need to type a reply of a number code to proceed in the game. For example, you might be presented with the phrase "Chatsubo" "Ratz" "Chiba City". The player would rotate the wheel layers such that the first two phrases (around the outer edge) line up. Then the user would read the number that appears inside the box with the label for the third phrase word(s). Type in the number and game continues.
There are a few [web hosted "code wheels"](http://www.mlsite.net/neuro/) as the lookup table for the wheel has been well documented for a while. I even wrote a simple [Neuromancer code lookup in JavaFX](https://github.com/maehem/neuromancer-pax-wheel) and might optionally incorporate it into the game at some point. While I could recap what the phenomena Neuromancer PC is, there are numerous sites and YouTube videos with descriptions, walk-throughs and commentary. Here's a list of a few that I find interesting: - [SmallInteger - Text Walkthrough](https://www.smallinteger.com/random/neuromancer.txt) - [Walkthrough King - Text Walkthrough](https://www.walkthroughking.com/text/neuromancer.aspx) - [Adventurer's Guild - Walkthrough with screenshots](https://advgamer.blogspot.com/2013/05/game-32-neuromancer-learning-ropes.html) - [AMC_revived - Very Thorough and Recent Walkthrough](https://gamefaqs.gamespot.com/pc/564806-neuromancer/faqs/81175) There are also some wonderful YouTube playthroughs. All of them were helpful with information regarding my development efforts. - [Julia Minamata - Let’s Play Series](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7_1X038QoG8) - [DarkwyndPT - Long Playthrough](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=l6FEqvhp-d0) - [Hipolito Pichardo - Neuromancer game ending - Adventure Quest #33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5RtJPn7a_Cs) - [MemorySectorZero - Extensive Cyberspace playthroughs on AppleII](https://www.youtube.com/@MemorySectorZero/videos) ## What makes this interesting for you? In a nutshell, I was hooked when I first read the Neuromancer book. I had just graduated college, I was already a CompuServe dial-up service junkie and even spent time on a few dial-up BBSs. I had seen Neuromancer released on C64 sometime in early 1989 or even 1988, but I didn't own a Commodore 64 or even a desktop PC at the time. However, by 1990, I was on my second job out of college at none other than [Sun Microsystems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Microsystems), who were leaders in the design and manufacture of early internet hardware. Sun was already directly on the new thing called the Internet and had state-of-the-art hardware called "workstations" that put PCs to shame. As employees, we had email (still a new thing) and access to a thing called Usenet, kind of a text version of web pages, where vast information was searchable and groups of like-minded people could group and share ideas and information about subjects they were interested in. Similar to BBSs of the previous decade except no dial-up (always connected) and the places you could explore expanded every day. The Neuromancer game was somewhat modeled after this. The player would find a public terminal and simply connect to get email, BBS or banking. When the player finally had some hardware, they could find instead, a "Jack" and gain access to a graphical version of cyberspace, where they could navigate, forward-back, left-right to sites and access more important types of information. Instead of passwords, cyberspace sites had "ICE" that the user would battle with in a turn based manner until they died or the site ICE was smashed through. Once through, the player could access the site via a BBS style terminal interface and download more powerful tools to battle the next ICE with. They might also peruse the site to gain hints and information about where to go next in the game.
I thought this made a wonderful metaphor for how I'd already been accessing the real internet already. In my mind the internet felt like some kind of ocean to be explored, I spend many on work and off work hours using the internet at my terminal there. At the time, the Matrix presented in the game, as well as the book, felt like a plausible approach for an actual future internet. Virtual Reality (VR) was emerging as an idea back then as well and even got involved as an engineer in it while working at Sun. VR's promise was something like "headphones for your eyes". But I think for it's time, it was a harder problem than any of us thought. Here we are 35 years later and Meta and others still have work to do. All in all, I was sucked completely in by cyberpunk and with a strong bias towards the techicnal how-it-worked and how it could work. For all the corny and trope-ish things found in Neuromancer PC game, I feel that they got a lot right in regards to how I viewed the preset and the possible future back in 1989... and still do. ## What does it do? Currently, this software is able to play the game as well as uncompress, decode and browse the image and text game assets from Neuromancer PC .DAT files. You will need a copy of the original floppy files, I won't distribute them here. Many abandon-ware sites have archived them. Once running, the application will scan your NEURO1.DAT and NEURO2.DAT files, extract and cache the assets to your user computer. You can then use the browser function to explore the sprites, backgrounds, animations and dialog text. As of early 2026 the game is now playable. I would call it "late Alpha" quality as most required features are present and most game goals are achievable. However, some things might not yet work at all or at least appear to be glitchy. The updside is that the game save file is plain text and human readable. In dire circumstances, one could edit the game save file to get past any hinderance. # Is this an emulator for the game? Not really... This game uses the original content but the engine is 100% brand new! Written in Java/JavaFX, the game mode accesses the cached game content and attempts to present an experience that is 99% like the DOS version from 1989. No attempt was made to understand how the original DOS executable operated. # But why? Of all the games I've played on the PC, this was one I really enjoyed. Since I don't really program professionaly anymore, I do like to keep my programming skills "fresh". I do that by setting challenges to myself based on personal interests. So for this excerise, I chose to deep-dive into the internals of Neuromancer PC and see where it lead me. Once I had the game assets decoded, I felt a strong pull to see how far I could get using those assets in my own "game engine". Step by step I recreated the experience of the original DOS game. In the process, this required me to research and code many aspects of Java/JavaFX I had not yet learned about (or had forgotten). So after about two months of writing this "emulator", I present a somewhat working version of the game. It has many rough edges and the end-game portion is missing, but it is largely playable. # Can I be a tester? Yes! You can try Javamancer out and submit issues. But, if you have not played the original, please do that first. The bugs and issues (and peering at the source code) of this remake would probably spoil the entertainment aspect of the game. So for first timers, please find something like "DOS Box" and images of the game's .DAT files and experience as much of the game as you can there. Use any of the "game walkthrough" sites out there to navigate the game when you get stuck. Once you've had your fill, come back here and do it again on this Java version. Using the GIT Hub "Issues" feature, please note any issues you have with playing the game. Over time, I'll target these issues and make the game feel as close to the original as I can. # Can I contribute code? If you have Java/JavaFX skills, please feel free to fork and contribute fixes to the code. I'll try to integrate fixes as they come in. # Will there be a downloadable version of the game? Yes. in the future. I'm looking at various ways to distrubute the game. Right now I'm considering the most "hacker" way of doing this by only making it only available on command-line tools like "Brew" and "apt-get". # Where did you get the idea for this? This game had such an impact on me in 1989 that I longed for something like it all the time it since then. Fast forward to 2010, I was in between projects and toyed with the idea of creating a Neuromancer-like game using HTML-5, which was newfangled around that time. I did a few coding experiments but didn't make any real progress. Plus, of course, a paying project came to me and I had to abandon all fun projects for a while. A few years later, I had the idea to poke around the original game files with a hex editor, and while I could see small bits of interesting things, I never was able to make any real progress on the games asset secrets. I would try that experiment a few more times over the next decade. During that time I discovered DOSBox which ran well on MacOS and would occasionally make my way through the original game, just like the old times. Around 2020 (perhaps during covid lock-down) I had, again the wild notion to extract the data from the original files and maybe do something with them. I really liked playing the game in a DOS emulator, but wished there was a way to play it directly on something more modern and maybe even be able to add things to or change things (like imagery) in the game. I initially probed around the DAT files with a hex editor, again, but my knowledge of old game encoding and compression were lacking. I really couldn't make sense of it so I gave up. A few months later, I had the idea of coding something similar from scratch. I had a new idea to make a Neuromancer-like game with my own characters but set in a very similar world (hacking, BBS, Matrix ICE busting, etc.). So I started some JavaFX object oriented code game-engine experiments with a "room" where a character could walk around, talk to a NPC, had a simple inventory. I worked out these constraints over a few months and ended up with a game app that was rough but pleasing. It was the idea I had dremt up back in 2010 and had attempted in HTML. But this time I was able to make much more progress by going with Java/JavaFX, which I used quite considerably professionally up till then. I started to add rooms to the experiment and soon had a multi room area that the player could walk room to room and affect the environment. I now had my own simple game engine. I also started making notes for my own character and setting. Like in Neuromancer PC, my character starts with nothing and the NPCs drop hints about what to do next. My setting is also in a cyberpunk future but set in the American South West (go with what you know). Different challenges than Chiba City and a character named "Jack". "Jack" was running on my new engine called "Abyss". But then it occurred to me if I could remake Neuromancer PC in the new Abyss engine (entitled Chiba City Blues)? ### Abyss engine (my next engine) running a Neuromancer remake A little rough around the edges, but a running game on the "[Abyss](https://github.com/maehem/Abyss)" engine. Left: My version of Chatsubo Bar. Right: My take on the Cyberspace interface. I'm still working with an artist for character designs and such. This is all prototype stuff so don't judge.

## One project became three... During this process, I'd realized that I now had three projects to juggle. A Neuromancer PC clone "[Chiba City Blues](https://github.com/maehem/ChibaCityBlues)", my game story idea "Jack" and the underlying engine "Abyss". So I divided the work up such that both "Neuro-clone" and "Jack" ran on the same game engine, called "[Abyss](https://github.com/maehem/Abyss)". I've been working on those three projects for about five years now, no rush. BUT... Javamancer is not any of those things, so now I have four related projects. ## Fast forward to 2024 and the creation of Javamancer In researcing more for "Chiba City Blues" I ran across the work of [Henadzi Matuts](https://habr.com/en/articles/352050/) . Hendazi had the same initial curiosity but did exactly what I couldn't, he used his skills in 8088/8086 assembler to reverse engineer the Neuromancer PC game byte by byte. He went further and wrote a series of four amazing blog posts that break down the asset encoding on the original Neuromancer PC game DAT files. He had done it back in 2018, but somehow I had not stumbled across his work until 2024. However, he decided to try porting Neuromancer PC to Windows (64-bit) in C++. But his detailed study of the game's data was eye opening for me. As a bonus, he had released his work as MIT license. Since I planned to rewrite parts of what he did in a different language (Java) it made attribution much easier. Hendazi is credited at the top of each of my source files, also MIT license. I've included Handazi's code here in my source tree for reference. I've made no changes (except for an additional note or comment here and there). But if you want to study Hendazi's code, I suggest you go straight to their source at: [Hendazi Matut's Reuromancer](https://github.com/HenadziMatuts/Reuromancer) Handazi's Blogs are in Russian, so I suggest you use Chrome to view them and let Google translate it for you. From there, I was able to unpack and decode all the assets, in Java, in a couple weeks. So here is "Javamancer" in it's current evolving state. I'm sure there are issues and it comes with no instructions. You'll probably need the latest Netbeans and Java to run it. ![Screenshot of Javamancer Resource Browser showing a game asset background of PIC format.](/images/javamancer-browser-pic.png) # Other Mentions In this process, I ran across a wonderful cross-platform tool called [imHex](https://github.com/WerWolv/ImHex) . It was invaluable in probing the decoded data from the DAT files as well as debugging my custom PNG encoder. ## License MIT License
